comparison: Strong agreement on AlphaFold2 methodology (C34-C44). Both evaluations find the computational approach well-defined and validated. OpenEval emphasizes threshold selection and ranking confidence metrics, while peer reviewers affirm the overall methodological approach and its validation of known complexes.

Both address validation of known interactions (C45-C66, C49-C66 overlap). OpenEval emphasizes successful recovery of 7/13 known interactions with structural alignment, while peer reviewers implicitly accept these recapitulated interactions as confirming AlphaFold2 effectiveness. Both treat this as strong validation.

Strong agreement on novel interaction validation (C67-C73). Both evaluations support the 60% validation rate (3/5) for novel predictions. OpenEval notes the germline-protein-free system and co-IP limitations, while peer reviewers explicitly validate these findings as a major strength without concerns about negative results.

Strong agreement on Spn-E_Squ structural characterization (C76-C90). OpenEval provides detailed assessment of structural predictions and computational consistency, while peer reviewers focus on the same claims. Both find the structural model well-supported, though OpenEval notes need for experimental interface validation.

Strong agreement on mutagenesis validation (C91-C99). Both evaluations affirm the experimental validation through salt bridge disruption. OpenEval emphasizes graded mutation effects and co-localization loss, while peer reviewers explicitly state this confirms functional significance of the predicted interface.

Both address higher-order complex predictions (C100-C103, C102-C108 overlap) with uncertainty. OpenEval finds the tetramer model speculative without experimental validation. Peer reviewers identify this as a weakness, noting that pairwise interactions are only a first step and higher-order complex analysis is incomplete.

Strong agreement on limitations of trimer predictions (C104-C108). Both evaluations express uncertainty about computational predictions of higher-order complexes. OpenEval notes discrepancy between predictions and observations, while peer reviewers emphasize that building larger complexes from pairwise interactions requires extension and validation.

Strong agreement on in vivo validation (C109-C113). Both evaluations support the ovarian tissue experiments and co-IP specificity. OpenEval emphasizes antibody specificity and selective co-IP patterns, while peer reviewers implicitly accept this as part of overall experimental confirmation without raising concerns.

Agreement on expanded screening (C120-C124). Both evaluations support the 17% validation rate (3/18) for oogenesis-related proteins. OpenEval notes lower success rate but biological plausibility, while peer reviewers acknowledge the expansion and validation without treating low rate as undermining the approach.

OpenEval evaluates Mei-W68 interaction (C125-C128) as uncertain due to speculative regulatory mechanism without functional assays. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for this specific interaction and its mechanistic implications.

Partial overlap on validation challenges (C134-C142, C134). OpenEval supports the Kd prediction filter as reasonable secondary screening. Peer reviewers acknowledge validation challenges (C134) as part of the expanded screening context but don't specifically evaluate the Kd filtering approach.

Strong agreement on genome-wide Piwi screen (C143-C153, C144-C153 overlap). Both evaluations support the comprehensive screening of ~12,000 proteins identifying 164 partners. OpenEval emphasizes the 1.5% hit rate as consistent with biological expectations, while peer reviewers treat this large-scale prediction as a major contribution.

Partial overlap on Arx identification (C154-C165, C154/C157). Both evaluations support Arx as a high-confidence hit. OpenEval addresses paralog predictions and negative functional results, interpreting them as pseudogenes or redundancy. Peer reviewers acknowledge Arx within the broader Piwi screen context.

Partial overlap on high-confidence predictions (C166-C168, C167). Both evaluations support validated predictions against known biology. OpenEval emphasizes mechanistic inference about substrate positioning, while peer reviewers include this within the broader genome-wide screening results.

Partial overlap on uncharacterized protein family (C169-C173, C170). OpenEval expresses uncertainty due to lack of expression and speculative stress-induced function. Peer reviewers include this within genome-wide screening but don't specifically evaluate the uncertainty around expression conditions.

Partial overlap on validation limitations (C174-C177, C174-C176). Both evaluations support demonstration that similar confidence scores yield different outcomes. OpenEval emphasizes this shows computational limitations, while peer reviewers include this as part of the broader Piwi screening results.

Agreement on method limitations and caveats (C178-C184, C178-C179 overlap). Both evaluations support appropriate acknowledgment of computational limitations. OpenEval emphasizes importance of biological context and value for specific use cases, while peer reviewers implicitly accept limitations as appropriately stated.

Strong agreement on overall study significance (C15-C119, C29/C114-C116/C183-C184 overlap). Both evaluations affirm the value of bridging computational predictions with experimental validation. OpenEval supports the systematic methodology, while peer reviewers explicitly state this demonstrates how in silico approaches can streamline identification of novel interactions.
